# KV Cache: Technical Overview

## What It Is

KV cache is a memory optimization technique used in transformer-based language models during autoregressive generation. When a model processes text, each token position produces two critical values: a Key vector and a Value vector. These vectors are computed through matrix multiplications involving the token's embedding and the model's weight matrices. The KV cache stores these computed Key and Value tensors so they don't need to be recalculated from scratch for every new token generated.

During standard inference, a model processes an input prompt by computing attention across all tokens simultaneously. For autoregressive generation—where tokens are produced one at a time—the previously computed keys and values remain relevant because future tokens attend to all preceding positions. Without caching, the model would recompute the entire forward pass for every single token output, dramatically increasing computational cost.

## How It Works

At each generation step, the model receives the newly emitted token and computes its Query, Key, and Value projections. Rather than discarding the Key and Value after computing attention for that step, the system appends them to persistent caches stored in GPU memory. Subsequent steps retrieve these cached tensors alongside the new computation, allowing attention mechanisms to reference all prior context without redundant work.

This mechanism transforms the computational complexity of sequence generation. A naive approach scales as O(n² × d) for n tokens and hidden dimension d, since each new token attends to all previous tokens and requires full reprocessing. # KV Cache: Enabling Efficient Long-Context Inference

## What Is KV Cache?

In transformer-based language models, self-attention requires each token to attend to all previous tokens during generation. For every output token, the model computes attention scores between the current position and all prior positions, retrieving the corresponding key (K) and value (V) vectors from each earlier token. Without caching, these K and V vectors would need to be recomputed from scratch at every decoding step—an expensive operation that scales quadratically with sequence length.

KV cache solves this by storing the computed key and value vectors for all previously processed tokens in memory after their initial forward pass. During autoregressive generation, new tokens only need to compute their own K/V projections once, then append them to the existing cache. Subsequent tokens retrieve pre-computed values rather than recalculating them, reducing per-token computation from O(n·d) to O(d), where n is context length and d is the hidden dimension.

## Why It Matters for Long Context

As context windows expand toward 128K tokens and beyond, the computational savings from KV caching become critical. Without caching, inference time grows prohibitively slow because each generated token must reprocess the entire prefix. KV caching transforms this relationship, making longer contexts computationally viable by ensuring that past tokens are processed exactly once while future tokens are generated efficiently.

Beyond raw performance, KV caching enables several architectural innovations. Techniques like grouped-query attention (GQA) and multi-head latent attention reduce the number of unique K/V pairs stored without sacrificing quality, further improving efficiency. Sliding window attention and persistent cache strategies build on KV caching foundations to handle effectively infinite contexts within bounded memory budgets.

For applications requiring extended reasoning—document summarization, multi-turn conversations, code analysis with large repositories—KV caching is what makes real-time interaction with lengthy contexts achievable.
